title: He will come again (CCC 668–682)
hook: Christ reigns now and will come in glory

segments.voice: Yesterday, he descended: Holy Saturday, and Christ going down among the dead to look for Adam. Your line was even the dead heard. Did you hear a story about someone who came before you? Day one thousand seventy-eight.

A group of friends on a hillside outside Jerusalem, heads tipped back, staring at the sky. A cloud has just taken Jesus out of their sight, and they can't stop looking at the place where he was. Then two men in white are standing beside them, and their question is almost funny. In the Douay-Rheims: "Ye men of Galilee, why stand you looking up to heaven? This Jesus who is taken up from you into heaven, shall so come, as you have seen him going into heaven." Stop staring, in other words. He's coming back. Now go. Today's word is the Church's name for that coming.
screen: `HEADS TIPPED BACK.` → `WHY STAND YOU LOOKING UP?` → `HE SHALL SO COME.`

segments.voice: Parousia is the Church's word, taken from Greek, for Christ's return in glory at the end of time. But the section opens somewhere you might not expect. Not with the end, with now. Christ already reigns, the Catechism says. Since his ascension he is Lord of the world and of history, and his kingdom is already present, in mystery, in the Church, which it calls the seed and beginning of that kingdom on earth. So Catholics live in a strange in-between: the king already crowned, the kingdom not yet complete. Already, and not yet. The Catechism is frank that this in-between is not peaceful. The kingdom is still under attack by evil, it says, and the Church will pass through a final trial before the end. Then comes a line that leaves no room for a calendar. The time of his coming is not known. Jesus says in the Gospels that no one knows the day or the hour, and in Acts he tells the disciples it is not for them to know the times the Father has set. And when he comes, the Creed says, it will be to judge the living and the dead; the Catechism adds that the secrets of hearts will be brought to light. Meanwhile, the Church waits, and the waiting has words. Near the very end of the Bible, Christ's promise gets an answer, in the Douay-Rheims: "Surely I come quickly: Amen. Come, Lord Jesus." Catholics hear the same hope at Mass, just after the Our Father, in a prayer that speaks of awaiting the coming of our Savior.
screen: `CHRIST ALREADY REIGNS.` · `ALREADY, AND NOT YET.` · `THE DAY AND THE HOUR: UNKNOWN.` · `TO JUDGE THE LIVING AND THE DEAD.` · then, large: `COME, LORD JESUS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: live today as if he's coming. Not in a panic. More like a household expecting a guest it loves. Settle, and breathe. Look around the day ahead the way you'd look around a room before someone arrives. Is there a word you'd want to take back? A call you'd want to make? A small mess you'd want set right? Choose one. Just one. If you pray, you can say the words near the Bible's end: come, Lord Jesus. If you don't, let the guest be anyone you'd be glad to see walk in. The bell holds the time.

Parousia. Christ's coming in glory at the end of time; he reigns already, and the day is not known. This week: soul, Christ, the virginal conception, the hidden life, Pilate, the descent, and now this. Today's word.
Your line: he will come. Today, set right the one thing you chose, the word, the call, or the mess, before the evening comes. Day one thousand seventy-eight.

howItsDone: Catholics profess at Mass that Christ "will come again in glory to judge the living and the dead," and the season of Advent keeps both his first coming and his return in view.

CCC paraphrased: Christ already reigns (668), Church as seed and beginning of the kingdom, present in mystery (669), kingdom still under attack (671), time not known (673), final trial (675), judgment and secrets of hearts (678–679).
'Parousia is a Greek word the New Testament uses for Christ's coming' (e.g. Matthew 24:27; 1 Thessalonians 4:15): a fact about the Greek text, not an etymology. Confirm.
Mass embolism phrase ('waiting in joyful hope for the coming of our Savior') given in current English without quotation marks: copyrighted ICEL text, used only as a short reference. Keeper may cut.
'A line that leaves no room for a calendar' refers to date-setting, not to a belief; Keeper may cut.
Week end (days 1072–1078): look-back placed in the teach's last line and the word segment.

Editor: 'waiting in joyful hope' is the pre-2011 Mass wording, so the line is now a paraphrase; cut the uncited claim about New Testament usage of parousia; removed the duplicate week look-back from the teach (kept in the word segment).

Audit: factual fix. Apocalypse 22:20 is not the Bible's last words (22:21, the grace, follows), so the teach, the match pair and the trapdoor no longer call it the last words. Acts 1:11 and Apocalypse 22:20 Challoner wording checked.
